title: MB7-18907
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The refugee protection claimant, XXXX XXXX, is a citizen of Haiti and is claiming refugee protection under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

In ruling on this refugee protection claim, the panel took into account the Chairperson's Guideline 9: Proceedings Before the IRB Involving Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity and Expression.1 ALLEGATIONS

The claimant was born on XXXX XXXX, 1959, in XXXX, Haiti. He states that on his birthday on XXXX XXXX, 1984, an XXXX priest named XXXX XXXX summoned him into the rectory and promised him a US visa and money in exchange for sexual relations with him. The claimant accepted. After that first meeting, the claimant continued to go to the rectory and developed a homosexual relationship with the priest.

The claimant states that he was bullied by his peers and that they beat him when he went to the rectory and called him "masi."2 On XXXX XXXX, 1985, the claimant left his village for Port-au-Prince, where he continued to practise homosexuality. In his neighbourhood, people called him "masi." On XXXX XXXX, 1987, he was physically assaulted by three strangers, who called him "masi." The claimant felt increasingly in danger, which is why he was living common-law with a woman. He left Haiti for the Bahamas on XXXX XXXX, 1998.

In 2006, in the Bahamas, he married XXXX XXXX XXXX, who was not aware of his sexual orientation. He states that he continued to practise homosexuality in secrecy. However, in the streets and at work, he was bullied and verbally assaulted because of his sexual orientation. On XXXX XXXX, 2017, he was assaulted. During the fight, he lost his wallet and driver's licence. He reported this incident to the police, who wrote him a report and told him, "I am not interesting in your gay business I wish the kill you and you better stop your stupidity." He decided to leave the Bahamas and arrived in the United States on XXXX XXXX, 2017. He arrived in Canada on October 12, 2017, and filed a claim for protection at Fort Erie.

After considering the documentary and testimonial evidence, the panel concludes that the claimant is a person referred to in Article 1E of the United Nations Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees (the Convention).

Moreover, the panel determines that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee" under section 96 of the IRPA or a "person in need of protection" under subsection 97(1) of the IRPA, for the reasons that follow. Exclusion under Article 1E

On October 18, 2018, the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada (IRB) received a Minister's opinion regarding a possible exclusion based on Article 1E of the Convention, given that it appears from the claimant's file that he was granted permanent residence in the Bahamas, as indicated by the stamp on page 27 of his Haitian passport3 XXXX and his permanent residence certificate4 issued on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2012.
According to section 98 of the IRPA, "[a] person referred to in section E or F of Article 1 of the Refugee Convention is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection."

Section E of Article 1 of the Convention is included in a schedule to the IRPA and reads as follows: E. This Convention shall not apply to a person who is recognized by the competent authorities of the country in which he has taken residence as having the rights and obligations which are attached to the possession of the nationality of that country.

In her notice of intervention,5 sent to the IRB and to the claimant, the Minister's representative submits that the information on the record demonstrates that: [translation] a. Section E of Article 1 of the Refugee Convention applies to the claimant because the evidence on the record shows that he has a status in the Bahamas that confers on him rights that are substantially similar to those of Bahamian nationals.

The Minister's representative submits that the evidence establishes a prima facie case that the claimant has permanent resident status in the Bahamas and is therefore excluded from the application of the Convention. Moreover, the Minister's representative considers that voluntarily abandoning his permanent resident status in the Bahamas is not the behaviour of someone who allegedly fears returning to Haiti. She further states that asylum shopping is incompatible with the surrogate dimension of international refugee protection.

Furthermore, the Minister's representative is of the opinion that the significant number of trips to Haiti (Haitian entry and exit stamps in the claimant's passport) that the claimant has made since he left the country in XXXX 1998 raise legitimate questions about his subjective fear, his credibility and the merits of his claim for refugee protection. Moreover, the Minister's representative submits that the claimant himself stated in his sworn statement to a border services officer at the port of entry that he does not fear returning to Haiti or to the Bahamas. For these reasons, she is asking the panel to reject his refugee protection claim.

During the hearing, the panel asked the claimant what his status in the Bahamas was, and he stated that he was a resident. The panel asked him what kind of residence permit he had, and he responded that he had a work permit. The panel then reminded him that his residence certificate states that he is a permanent resident of the Bahamas. He confirmed that he was a permanent resident of the Bahamas. The panel asked him whether, at the time of the hearing, his status was still valid, and the claimant answered that it was. First, the panel would like to point out that the claimant did not give a direct answer to the question about the kind of residence permit that he had in that country, and the panel therefore draws a negative inference regarding his credibility. Second, the panel notes that on the day of his hearing, the claimant was still a permanent resident of the Bahamas.

In light of the claimant's testimony, the panel concludes prima facie that the claimant has permanent resident status in the Bahamas, which gives him rights and obligations that are substantially similar to those of Bahamian nationals, including health care, education and employment rights.
In light of the foregoing and having analyzed the evidence, the panel concludes that the claimant is a person referred to in Article 1E of the Convention.
First, the panel must determine whether the claimant can be excluded under Article 1E of the Convention because he is a permanent resident of the Bahamas.
Second, if the claimant cannot return to the Bahamas, the panel will examine his claim based on his country of nationality, Haiti. Identity
The panel is satisfied as to the claimant's identity as a citizen of Haiti, which was established by means of his testimony, as well as a copy of his passport issued by the Haitian authorities.6

The claimant also submitted evidence to establish his permanent resident status in the Bahamas.7 After examining these documents, the panel concludes that the claimant has established that he is a permanent resident of the Bahamas. Credibility

When claimants swear that certain facts are true, this creates a presumption that they are true,8 unless there are valid reasons to doubt their truthfulness. The finding of whether or not a claimant's evidence is credible is made on a balance of probabilities.

There were significant omissions and inconsistencies in the claimant's testimony about his alleged fears in the Bahamas. Moreover, his behaviour is inconsistent with that of a person who allegedly fears persecution in the Bahamas by reason of his sexual orientation. The claimant's problems in his village, XXXX, in 1985

At the hearing, the claimant stated that he first had sexual relations with a man on XXXX XXXX, 1984, with the XXXX priest in his village, XXXX. He also stated that the relationship with the village priest lasted from XXXX to XXXX 1985. He stated that people started to suspect that he and the priest were having sexual relations in late XXXX or early XXXX 1985 and that the suspicions caused problems for him. He was insulted, involved in fights and had rocks thrown at him. He alleged that people figured out that they were having sexual relations because the priest was effeminate. The panel asked him when he had left the village, to which he answered XXXX 1985. The panel asked if he had lived in the village the entire time from XXXX 1985 to XXXX 1985; he answered no and stated that he went to Port-au-Prince for school and came back to the village during vacation periods. The panel asked him why he had continued to return to a place where he was in danger. He stated that it was because no one suspected them. The panel noted that, according to his testimony, people started getting suspicious in late XXXX or early XXXX 1985, yet he continued to go back and forth between his village and Port-au-Prince until XXXX 1985. He repeated that at the time no one suspected them. He also stated that he had left his village for good on XXXX XXXX, 1985, following a [translation] "big fight." The tribunal pointed out that in his account, the claimant did not specify that he left his village on XXXX XXXX, 1985, following a "big fight." The claimant stated that he had said this. The panel noted that it was not written in his story. The claimant stated, [translation] "I know it's in there." The panel pointed out once again that the claimant had not mentioned in his account that the reason he had left his village was a "big fight." He stated that XXXX and XXXX were starting to give him trouble. The panel then noted that the claimant had stated that everything in his account was true, complete and correct and that the part about a "big fight" on XXXX XXXX, 1985, was not in it. The claimant asked to reread his account, but the panel did not allow him to reread it. First, the panel has reasonable grounds to believe that if the claimant had to leave his village in XXXX 1985 because of a "big fight," he would have mentioned this in his account. For that reason, the panel draws a negative inference concerning the claimant's credibility and the problems he allegedly had in his village because of his sexual orientation. Second, the panel draws a further negative inference regarding the claimant's subjective fear because he did not provide a reasonable explanation for returning to his village from XXXX 1985 to XXXX 1985, when according to his testimony, his troubles in the village started in late XXXX or early XXXX 1985. The romantic relationship with Mr. XXXX in the Bahamas

At the hearing, the panel asked the claimant if he had had any romantic relationships with men. He answered yes-a first relationship with the priest in Haiti in 1985 and a second with Mr. XXXX in the Bahamas in 2008. The panel asked him how long his relationship with Mr. XXXX had lasted, to which he answered that it had lasted eight years and that during those eight years, they had lived together in Nassau. The panel asked the claimant why he had not mentioned Mr. XXXX in his account. He stated that he was homosexual in the Bahamas, but had not mentioned Mr. XXXX. The panel repeated the question, and the claimant responded that he had not put it down on paper. The panel asked him why he had not mentioned Mr. XXXX in his account. He answered [translation] "for no reason" and stated that he had indicated that he was homosexual, but had not mentioned Mr. XXXX or written his name down on the paper. The panel finds it hard to believe that the claimant would have had a romantic relationship with Mr. XXXX and lived with him for eight years in the Bahamas, yet forgotten to mention their romantic relationship in his account. The panel makes a negative finding regarding the claimant's overall credibility with regard to his fears stemming from his sexual orientation. The assault of XXXX XXXX, 2017

In his Basis of Claim Form and at the hearing, the claimant stated that he was assaulted on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017, in the Bahamas by a group of individuals who called him a homosexual. He tried to get away by walking really fast, but the individuals allegedly followed him, beat him up and tried to kill him. They stole everything he was carrying in his pockets. The claimant stated that he told them he was not homosexual, to which they answered that they knew he was because they knew that his wife had left him and they knew him well. That same day, he filed a complaint with the police and a report9 was provided at the hearing. The panel asked him to confirm that the assault took place on XXXX XXXX, 2017, and that he had filed a complaint with the police that day; the claimant responded yes. The panel then noted that the report was prepared on XXXX XXXX, 2017. It states that [translation] "[the claimant] was approached last month by strangers who assaulted him because of his sexual orientation." The panel asked the claimant to explain this inconsistency in the evidence presented. The claimant stated that he had brought this paper from the Bahamas. The panel repeated the question, and the claimant repeated that he had brought the document from the Bahamas. When his counsel asked him why the police report stated that the assault had taken place sometime in XXXX 2017, and not on XXXX XXXX, 2017, the claimant responded that that was how the officer had written it down. In the panel's opinion, this answer is not satisfactory because if the assault had taken place on XXXX XXXX, 2017, that would have been reflected in the police report. The panel finds it reasonable to believe that an officer who takes the time to write a police report explaining events would also take the time to note when they occurred, especially if the incident took place the same day. For that reason, the panel draws a negative inference concerning the claimant's credibility with respect to the alleged attack on him on XXXX XXXX, 2017, in the Bahamas. Furthermore, the panel gives no weight to the police report to corroborate the attack on XXXX XXXX, 2017, allegedly because of the claimant's sexual orientation. The marriage certificate

At the hearing, the claimant stated that he got married on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2006. The panel asked him his wife's name, to which he answered that her maiden name was XXXX XXXX XXXX, but that it is now XXXX XXXX XXXX. The panel asked him his wife's date of birth. He stated that she was born on XXXX XXXX, 1954, and that they also got married on XXXX XXXX. The panel then noted that, according to their marriage certificate (Exhibit C-2),10 they got married on XXXX XXXX, 2006. The claimant appeared uncomfortable and stated, [translation] "Oh well, I forgot the date. It is the XXXX." The panel noted that the claimant had just stated that they got married on his wife's birthday, and he stated that he thought it was XXXX XXXX. The panel asked him how old he was when he got married in 2006. He stated that he was 42, then that he was 40 and ended up stating that he was 42 years old. The panel repeated the question, and the claimant responded that he was 42 years old. The panel then pointed out that he was 47 in 2006. The claimant did not know what to say. The tribunal asked him why his marriage certificate indicates that he was 42, when he was born in 1959 and got married in 2006. The claimant seemed embarrassed and stated that he had noticed it too and thought that it was his age. The panel finds that the claimant adjusted his answers based on the contradictions and therefore draws a negative inference regarding his credibility.

At the hearing, the panel saw three different versions of the marriage certificate: * A first photocopy of the marriage certificate provided prior to the hearing (Exhibit C-2).11 The certificate number in the upper-right corner is XXXX. On this photocopy, it is written that the person who performed the marriage was the "Registrar General, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX." * The original marriage certificate provided by the claimant at the hearing (Exhibit C-9).12 The certificate number appearing in the upper-right corner is XXXX. This document states that the person who performed the marriage was the "Registrar General, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX." * A second photocopy of the marriage certificate provided by the claimant at the hearing (Exhibit C-8).13 This photocopy does not have a certificate number in the upper-right corner. On this photocopy, it states that the person who performed the marriage was the "Deputy Registrar, XXXX XXXX."

At the hearing, the claimant confirmed that he had brought these documents with him to Canada. When asked to explain the inconsistencies in the certificate numbers in the upper-right corners of the documents, the claimant stated that he did not know what had happened. He then stated that he had not brought the original with him from the Bahamas, that he had left it with his wife and that these were photocopies. The panel repeated the question, and the claimant answered that he did not know anything.

The panel then asked the claimant to explain the inconsistencies concerning the person who performed the marriage and, once again, the claimant stated that he did not know, that it was his marriage certificate. Given all the inconsistencies between the original and the two photocopies of his marriage certificate that were provided, the panel is not satisfied that the claimant has provided acceptable documents establishing that he was married to XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX now XXXX XXXX XXXX. Furthermore, the panel draws a negative inference concerning the claimant's overall credibility from the fact that he provided documents that are not acceptable. The letter from the claimant's ex-wife

At the hearing, the panel asked the claimant when he and his wife had separated. He answered that it was when Ms. XXXX had found out that he was homosexual. He stated that they had separated in 2008 and added that his wife had written him a letter in which she states that he is homosexual. The claimant was confronted with the fact that during his interview with a Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) officer on October 12, 2017, when the officer asked him when he and his wife had separated, he answered, [translation] "2 - 3 years, but she talks with me all the time." He stated they have been separated since 2008 and that she lived in one place and he lived in another. The panel repeated the question, and the claimant stated that they had broken up in 2008, but that he did not give the CBSA officer a specific year. He also stated that he did not remember specific years, but that they were separated. The panel pointed out that there is a difference between being separated for 10 years and being separated for 2 to 3 years. He stated that they have been separated since 2008 and that when he stated at the border that it had been 2 or 3 years, that meant that it was a long time ago. The panel is not satisfied with the claimant's answers; despite being given opportunities to explain the inconsistency between his testimony at the hearing and his interview with the CBSA officer, his explanation is not reasonable. The claimant's credibility is again undermined.

The claimant provided a letter14 signed by XXXX XXXX XXXX. In this letter, Ms. XXXX states that she [translation] "found out that her husband [XXXX XXXX] is homosexual" and for this reason, she [translation] "wants the marriage dissolved." Given the concerns outlined in paragraphs 26, 27, 28 and 29 concerning the certificate of marriage to XXXX XXXX XXXX, and the concerns noted in paragraph 30 regarding the date he and Ms. XXXX separated, the panel gives no weight to this letter as corroboration of the claimant's sexual orientation.

The claimant also provided a letter15 signed by the Executive Director of the XXXX XXXX organization. Given the credibility issues described above, the panel finds that this document has no probative value. Subjective fear

During the hearing, the panel noted that the claimant had made a number of round trips to Haiti, always with a stopover in the United States. The claimant always returned to the Bahamas. These returns in 2009, 2010, 2013, 2014, 2015 and 2016 took place after 2008, the year when, according to his testimony, his problems in the Bahamas began, yet he never claimed protection in the United States. At the hearing, he stated that he did not claim protection in the United States because he did not know anyone there. He also stated at the hearing that he did not find any place to seek refuge and that it was when his sister told him that it was possible to claim protection in Canada that he decided to come here.

On this point, it is worth noting that the Federal Court has confirmed that it is reasonable to conclude that a claimant returning to the country where he or she feared persecution makes the existence of such a fear unlikely. The Federal Court states the following in Kabengele:16 It is quite proper for the Refugee Division to take the plaintiff's actions into account in assessing his subjective fear. It is reasonable for it to conclude that the fact that he returned to the country where he feared persecution makes the existence of such a fear unlikely.

The panel is of the opinion that the claimant's failure to claim asylum in the United States during his multiple stopovers there in 2009, 2010, 2013, 2014, 2015 and 2016 undermines the credibility of his subjective fear of returning to the Bahamas, which is determinative in the analysis of his fear under section 96 of the IRPA.

In summary, for all the foregoing reasons, the panel does not believe that there is enough evidence in this case to establish that the claimant would have a reasonable fear of persecution by reason of his sexual orientation if he were to return to the Bahamas.

Considering all of the evidence, the panel concludes that the claimant, XXXX XXXX, is excluded under Article 1E of the United Nations Refugee Convention, because he has permanent resident status in the Bahamas, which gives him the rights and obligations that are attached to possession of that country's nationality, and he may return there and live there.

Consequently, pursuant to section 98 of the IRPA, since the claimant is a person referred to in section E of Article 1 of the Convention, he is neither a "Convention refugee" nor a "person in need of protection."

For all the foregoing reasons, the panel determines that XXXX XXXX is excluded under the Convention.
